# Four Hundred and Ten

The water was at the third step and had been at the third step for nine days. Ilse counted the steps every morning on the way in, the way other people weighed themselves.

She left her boots in the silt in the lobby. Up the ladder, the second floor of the Marram exchange was dry and smelled of hot dust and warm copper, and three gulls sat in the dark of the stairwell waiting for her to go away. Her table stood under the window with a clear line to the door: tablet, headphones, a mug with a chip out of the rim, the crate of drives under her right elbow. Six weeks of salvage behind her and eleven weeks of it left. On the door, printed in 1998 in the flat vowels of the previous century: IN CASE OF FLOOD, DO NOT USE ELEVATOR. There was one elevator in Marram, and it had been in the harbor since February.

The county called the work unsent correspondence and paid her by the drive. Marram's trunk line had kept running nineteen months after the fiber went — an old buffer that held the calls the exchange could not route, and released them, slowly, into a town with no subscribers left on it. Ilse took them out one at a time and gave them numbers. That was the work. It was not a metaphor, though nobody at the Resilience Office had quite believed that. Six weeks in they sent a man to ask whether the archive might be put in the cloud. It had been raining for eleven days. The roof of the exchange was by then a rumor.

She wiped the tablet on her trousers and opened the day's seventh drive. A woman: "Tell him the fence is down, and he's going to be eighty." Ilse logged it, and the eight seconds it took, and the fact that it had been sent four times. Then a boy saying nothing at all for four minutes, breathing in a room with a window open and, far off, a football match.

Module seven came out of the east wall with a sound like a spoon in a jar. Salt had grown a white fur over the pins, and when she turned it in the light she saw that the fur was not fur but small exact trees, each one a crystal with branches. She wiped the screen where her thumb would be. Where she had touched it, a bloom came up on the glass and stayed. She scraped it off with a thumbnail and it came away dry, like scurf, and while she watched, it began to come back.

At 9:14 the buffer stamped something coming up the trunk.

It was not on a drive. It was coming through the line itself. Ilse put one earphone in, held the other against the jack, where the salt had crusted, and heard her own voice.

*Ilse. It's the ninth. The water's at the third step, I know. There are four hundred and ten of them in the east corridor, and they're not records. They're just people who got cut off. I've moved them upstairs. The seal's going in at eleven tonight, so if you're hearing this on this floor, you're weeks early. Go—*

She played it eleven times. The stamp put the call nine years, four months and some days ahead of her. She wiped at the screen with her sleeve, and the salt came up again under her sleeve.

What she had was this: a dry floor. A finished index. Her own voice on the other side of the seal, still in it, still doing it, not sorry. *Weeks early.* There was more time than she had thought. For six weeks she had left the county's book open on the table at six and gone back up the ladder at seven. That evening she put her boots on and did not go back up the ladder.

Her sister called at ten past nine, when Ilse was already in the room above the pharmacy.

"Four hundred and six," Wren said. "You said four hundred and six."

"I said four hundred and ten."

"You said—" Wren stopped. Wren had been packing the flat for a month. "You've finished them," she said, in the voice you use for a hospital.

"I said four hundred and ten," Ilse said, and went to bed and slept all the way through, which she had not done since March.

For three days she worked to six and stopped at six. On the third evening she carried the recorder into the east corridor and set it down beside the trunk. The crates stood along the wall where they had always stood. She sat on the floor, opened the log on her knees, and counted the names — she had never counted them; the log counted messages — by the blue light of the tablet: four hundred and ten. Four hundred and ten people, cut off. She had put every one of them in the index.

Then she took a pin to the jack and worked the crust out of it, and the crackle went out of the line as if a window had been shut somewhere.

*—home. Let the water have the rest of it. I've done the part that counted.*

Rain was easing on the roof above them. A long pause. Then, closer to the mouth:

*It's stopped raining. Go home, Ilse.*

All summer she had heard *upstairs* as a dry floor: a place ten years down where the work would be finished, where it would have been worth doing. There was no upstairs. There was a woman on the last night, wet to the elbow, giving the rest of it away, and the rest of it was only the counting.

Ilse put the pin back in her pocket and picked up the crates.

They went out to the hill in seven trips on the pharmacy's handcart. She put them in the old lifeboat house, above the water line of anything the sea had got round to yet, and the door still had a lock on it. The last one she set down gently. She peeled the last label off the county's roll and stuck it to the wood and wrote nothing on it.

Her recorder she left on top, and by the time she had her coat buttoned, salt had come up out of its port — white and branching, exact, in a shape like the street plan of Marram.

The gulls were back on the east breakwater. They had not been there in months. She watched them work the tide until she was cold. Then she went down the far side of the hill to Wren's, where the kitchen light was on.

Both deliverables are complete in `/tmp/claude-1000/.../07-creative-writing/`.

**"Four Hundred and Ten"** (STORY.md, 1,088 words plus title) is a close-third-person story about Ilse, an archivist digitizing unsent messages in a drowned Marram exchange, whose job is indexed to a county contract. A voice arrives through the live trunk line — nine years, four months ahead — in her own voice, promising that the work has been finished and the archive moved "upstairs." Only after she cleans crystallized salt out of the headphone jack does she hear the rest: "Let the water have the rest of it." Her reading flips from proof that the indexing was worth it to a woman on the last night, wet to the elbow, giving the archive away and telling her to go home — so she spends the night carrying the crates up to the lifeboat house on the hill, leaves the final crate label blank, and walks down the far side to her sister's kitchen light. The salt motif recurs five times across screen, drive pins, headphone jack, and recorder port (closing on a crystal shaped like Marram's street plan), with brief dry humor in the 1998 "DO NOT USE ELEVATOR" notice, the county's cloud question, and Wren's hospital voice; no dream, simulation, or villain monologue is used. **RESPONSE.md** holds the 3-sentence emotional-arc note, and both files were written only in the task directory with no network use.
